title: L2 review: EC2, S3 and Lambda by example
text:
Terms used on this page
From the course flashcards, grouped by topic. Practise them in quiz mode, or try the match game.

EC2 instances
Instance. A virtual machine you rent from AWS, billed per second for the time it runs. Stopping it ends the compute charge, but its EBS disk still bills.
Instance type. The size you pick when you launch an EC2 server: how many vCPUs and how much memory it has, how fast its network is, and whether it has its own local disk.
EBS volume. A disk an EC2 instance reaches over the network, as its main disk or an extra one. Its data survives a stop, and it bills per GB-month while it exists, even when the instance is stopped.
Security group. The rules that say what network traffic may reach an EC2 instance and what it may send out, by protocol, port and address. They do not decide what the instance may do with other AWS resources.
IAM policy. A JSON document that says which actions are allowed on which AWS resources. Attached to a role, it sets what anything using that role may do.


S3
S3. AWS’s object store. You reach each object over the network by its name inside a bucket, and the data stays with no server running.
Bucket. A named container in S3 that holds objects. Its name is part of every object’s address.
Object key. The full name of one stored file inside an S3 bucket. It is only a name, unrelated to the column a group-by or a join uses.
Prefix. The leading part of an object’s name, such as day=2012-06-14/. S3 lists objects by it, and the console’s folders are built from it; the general-purpose buckets we use have no real folders.


Lambda functions
Lambda function. The unit you deploy to AWS Lambda: your code and its settings, run each time a trigger fires. One setting, memory, also sets its CPU and its price per millisecond.
Execution role. The identity AWS takes on when it runs a Lambda function. It decides which resources the code may read or change.
Execution environment. The isolated space AWS sets up to run a Lambda function, with its memory and a temporary disk. AWS may reuse it for later calls and pauses it between them.
Cold start. The set-up before the first call in a new Lambda environment: AWS loads the code, then your code’s initialisation runs, such as opening connections and importing libraries.
Handler. The function in your code that Lambda calls on each invocation, taking event and context. Code outside it runs once per environment, so a client built there is reused.


Billing
Time shape of demand. When a workload asks for its resources across a day or a week: a steady rate, a daily rhythm, a burst, or a scheduled job. With the peak rate, it decides whether provisioned or usage-based billing is cheaper.
Provisioned capacity. Compute you pay for while it is allocated to you, used or not. Unlike pay-per-use compute, its charge continues when nothing runs.
Usage-based billing. Charges for measured work, such as each request or each millisecond a function runs. They stop when nothing runs; stored data and logs still cost money.
Idle test. The question to ask of each compute charge: does it bill while nothing runs? If yes, it is provisioned capacity. Storage and logs are counted separately.

title: L5 review: Spark on a cluster
section: How Spark divides and coordinates the work
text:
How Spark divides and coordinates the work

What does Spark run again when a core node is lost? *
A Spark query over a year of lift-gate scans in S3 counts the scans per gate, so its scan stage is followed by an Exchange (shuffle). The query runs on an EMR cluster of 1 primary and 2 core nodes, all m7g.xlarge, with the driver on core node 1. Each core node has an executor, a process that runs 4 tasks at a time (8 slots in total). The query’s scan stage has 36 tasks, each reading one Spark partition of the input: one or more byte ranges of the files in S3. The task counts just before the failure were:
scan stage, 36 tasks      finished   running   not started
core node 1                  10         4
core node 2                  10         4
total                        20         8           8
Then core node 2 fails, and its executor and its disk are lost.

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## After the core node 2 failure, besides the 8 tasks that have not started, how many scan tasks does Spark run again?

1. [x] 14
    > When core node 2 was lost, its 4 running tasks stopped and the output of its 10 finished tasks was also lost. Spark reruns the 14 tasks of core node 2, each rereading its Spark partition from S3; the output of core node 1's finished tasks stays available.
1. [ ] 4
    > Choosing 4 treats a finished task's output as safe. A finished scan task's output is stored on its node for the next stage; if the node is lost, the output is also lost, so Spark reruns the task.
1. [ ] 36
    > Choosing 36 reruns every task, as when a query in one process on one instance fails and is rerun from the start. Spark can reread the input's Spark partitions from S3, so it reruns only the tasks whose work was lost.
1. [ ] 28
    > Core node 1 still has its executor and its disk, so the output of its 10 finished tasks remains and its 4 running tasks continue. Only core node 2's work is lost.

Slide: 10 (also 8)

title: L5 review: Spark on a cluster
text:
Amazon EMR

How many tasks can the cluster run at once (how many slots does it have)?
An EMR cluster has three kinds of nodes, all m7g.xlarge with 4 vCPUs each, at $0.2227 an hour per node (on demand in ca-central-1, EC2 plus EMR’s fee):
primary   1 node
core      4 nodes
task      3 nodes
A node hosts at most one executor, which gets 4 cores, one per vCPU of the node, and so runs 4 tasks at a time (4 slots).

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## How many tasks can the cluster run at once (how many slots does it have)?

1. [x] 28
    > The 4 core nodes and 3 task nodes host executors, so 7 × 4 = 28 tasks run at once. The primary node manages the cluster and hosts no executor. You pay for 8 nodes, about \$1.78 an hour at \$0.2227 each, and 7 of them run tasks.
1. [ ] 32
    > Choosing 32 counts the primary node as a node that runs tasks. The primary node manages the cluster and hosts no executor.
1. [ ] 56
    > Choosing 56 gives each node 8 slots, two per vCPU. On our m7g nodes one vCPU is one physical processor core, and an executor gets one slot per vCPU: 4 per node.
1. [ ] 12
    > Choosing 12 assumes that only task nodes host executors. Core nodes also host executors and store blocks for the Hadoop Distributed File System (HDFS), while task nodes host executors without storing HDFS data.

Slide: 18, 19 (also 11, 16)

title: L5 review: Spark on a cluster
text:
Spark, PySpark and Spark SQL

What runs where: the plan, an action, or pandas on the driver
A notebook on an EMR cluster works with a bike-share company’s rides, stored as Parquet files on S3. Earlier cells left two DataFrames in the notebook:
per_city   Spark DataFrame    ride counts per city, built earlier
                              from the rides files
stations   pandas DataFrame   docks per station, with each station's city
F is pyspark.sql.functions.

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## For each line, what happens when its cell runs? Each option may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

- `rides = spark.read.parquet("s3://…/bikeshare/rides/")` :: Spark builds the plan on the driver; no ride rows are read
    > The driver lists the files and puts the read into the plan; a one-task job reads one file's footer to learn the columns, and no ride rows are read until an action needs them.
- `per_city.explain()` :: Spark builds the plan on the driver; no ride rows are read
    > `.explain()` prints the plan recorded so far on the driver and reads no ride rows, so no task starts. Spark scans the rows only when an action needs them.
- `victoria = per_city.filter(F.col("city") == "Victoria")` :: Spark builds the plan on the driver; no ride rows are read
    > `filter` is a transformation: Spark adds the step to the plan on the driver and reads no rows, and no task starts until an action needs the rows.
- `top = per_city.toPandas()` :: Spark sends tasks that read the ride rows; they run now
    > `toPandas()` is an action: it needs the rows of `per_city`, so the driver creates tasks from the plan and the executors read and count the rides now.
- `rows = per_city.collect()` :: Spark sends tasks that read the ride rows; they run now
    > `.collect()` is an action: it needs the rows of `per_city`, so the driver creates tasks from the plan and the executors read and count the rides now.
- `stations.groupby("city")["docks"].sum()` :: pandas computes on the driver; no task runs
    > `stations` is a pandas DataFrame, and pandas has no Spark plan: the sum is computed in the driver's Python process, and no executor gets a task.
- `top.to_csv("per_city.csv")`, after `top = per_city.toPandas()` has already run :: pandas computes on the driver; no task runs
    > `top` holds the rows that `toPandas()` already brought to the driver, so `top` is a pandas DataFrame with no Spark plan. The file is written from the driver's Python process, and no executor gets a task.
- :: pandas computes on the executors, split across them
    > A cluster does not split a pandas operation across executors. pandas runs in the driver's Python process and creates no Spark task.

A delivery company keeps its fees in one 1 GB Parquet file on S3. You have a PySpark notebook in JupyterHub open in your laptop’s browser, as in the lecture: Livy sends the notebook’s cells to the Spark driver. The notebook runs on an EMR cluster of 1 primary and 2 core nodes, all m7g.xlarge with 4 vCPUs and 16 GiB of memory each. A cell reads the file with pandas:
fees = pd.read_parquet("s3://…/delivery/fees.parquet")

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## Where are the rows of `fees` held, and what is the most memory the cell can use?

1. [x] In the driver's Python process, within one node's 16 GiB
    > Every cell of a PySpark notebook runs in the Spark driver. pandas works in the driver's Python process on one node, so the other nodes' memory does not help, and the process may be allocated less than the node's 16 GiB.
1. [ ] Across both core nodes' executors, within 32 GiB in total
    > Executors get work from Spark only through an action or the short job that reads a file's footer at `spark.read`. A pandas call is not Spark: no task is created, so the rows never leave the driver.
1. [ ] On your laptop, where the notebook is open, within its memory
    > Choosing the laptop assumes local Jupyter, where Python runs on your laptop. On EMR the browser only sends cells and shows output: JupyterHub is on the primary node, and the cells run in the driver on a core node, so the rows of `fees` stay on the cluster.

Slide: 22, 24, 25 (also 16, 21)


What goes into the Exchange (shuffle)?
A ferry company keeps its 2025 ticket sales as one Parquet file on S3. Each row is one ticket:



sale_date
route
fare




2025-03-02
Tsawwassen to Swartz Bay
$8


2025-03-02
Tsawwassen to Swartz Bay
$10


2025-03-05
Horseshoe Bay to Nanaimo
$18


…
…
…



A PySpark query computes the average fare per route for March 2025; sales is the Spark DataFrame read from the file and F is pyspark.sql.functions:
march = sales.filter(F.col("sale_date").between("2025-03-01", "2025-03-31"))
by_route = march.groupBy("route").agg(F.avg("fare").alias("avg_fare"))
Each scan task reads one Spark partition of the file: one or more byte ranges of the file. Tickets are stored in the order they were sold, so a route’s tickets are spread over several tasks. The Tsawwassen to Swartz Bay route sold 4 tickets in March, for $60 in all, so its average fare is $15. Two tasks read the 4 tickets:




tickets
fares
sum
average




task 1
3
$8, $10, $12
$30
$10


task 2
1
$30
$30
$30




---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## What should each task send into the `Exchange` (shuffle) so that the final stage computes \$15 from the least data?

1. [x] Count and sum of fares for the route
    > Task 1 sends 3 and \$30, task 2 sends 1 and \$30; the final stage adds them and divides: \$60 / 4 = \$15. Each task sends two numbers per route, however many tickets it reads. Partial totals are enough for a group-by sum, count or average; a window query or a join that regroups both tables by key sends every row into the `Exchange`, so one task receives all rows of each key.
1. [ ] Average of the task's fares for the route
    > The final stage would receive two averages, \$10 from task 1 and \$30 from task 2, and could only average them: (\$10 + \$30) / 2 = \$20, not \$15. The final stage cannot weight task 1's average by its 3 tickets because the count is not sent. An average of averages is wrong whenever the groups differ in size.
1. [ ] Every ticket row the task reads for the route
    > Sending every row into the `Exchange` also gives \$15, but sends more data. Partial totals give the same answer with two numbers per route from each task.

Slide: 27, 29

title: L5 review: Spark on a cluster
text:
Storage on the cluster

Where is each kind of data kept?
A team keeps Vancouver’s Van311 non-emergency service requests for 2025 as Parquet files on S3, and a notebook on an EMR cluster works with them:
cluster    1 primary + 2 core nodes
notebook   builds `late`, the requests that took more than 45 days to close
end        the cluster is terminated when the notebook's work ends

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## Where is each kind of data kept? Each option may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

- rows a task cannot fit in memory while it works :: the node's disk
    > Working data on a node's own disk is deleted when the cluster ends. A task that cannot fit its rows in memory spills them there and reads them back later.
- Spark's cache of a DataFrame once executor memory is full :: the node's disk
    > Working data on a node's own disk is deleted when the cluster ends. By default, Spark stores the cache in executor memory first and then on the node's disk once memory is full.
- the rows `.collect()` returns :: driver memory
    > The result is stored in the driver's process: the executors run the plan, and `.collect()` sends every row of the result to the driver.
- the number `late.count()` returns to the notebook :: driver memory
    > The result is stored in the driver's process: the executors run the plan and count the rows, and the driver receives the total as one Python number.
- the 2025 request files the notebook reads :: S3
    > The input was on S3 before the cluster started, and every executor reads its Spark partitions from there; S3 keeps the files after the cluster ends.
- the table of `late` requests that next week's report reads :: S3
    > The nodes' disks and HDFS are deleted with the cluster, so a result that next week's report reads is written to S3, which keeps it until someone deletes it.
- :: the cluster's HDFS
    > HDFS pools the core nodes' disks into one shared file system. A Spark job writes to HDFS only on purpose, such as a result the job rereads while the cluster runs, and HDFS is deleted with the cluster. Spills and Spark's cache go to the node's disk outside HDFS, and the table of late requests goes to S3 because next week's report reads it after the cluster is terminated. None of the listed data is stored in HDFS.

Slide: 32, 33 (also 16, 18, 24)

title: L5 review: Spark on a cluster
text:
Terms used on this page
From the course flashcards, grouped by topic. Practise the terms in quiz mode, or try the match game.

Spark: how a job runs
Driver. The program that coordinates a Spark application: it runs your code, builds the query plan and sends tasks to the executors.
Executor. A Spark program running on an EMR core or task node. It runs tasks and keeps their data in its memory or on the node’s disk.
Partition. A chunk of rows that one task processes as one unit. When reading files it holds one or more splits, each a byte range of one file, planned from the file sizes and the number of slots.
Task. One stage’s work on one chunk of rows, run in one slot: by default, one executor core.
Slot. One executor core, as room to run one task on one Spark partition at a time. An executor with 4 cores runs 4 tasks at once; our EMR nodes have one per vCPU.
Stage. A set of tasks Spark can run before rows have to move between partitions. Every task in it runs the same steps on a different partition.
Wave. The set of a stage’s tasks that run at the same time, one per slot. 36 reading tasks on 8 slots need 5 of them.
Transformation. A step such as filter or groupBy(...).count() that is only recorded in the plan. No task runs until an action asks for a result.
Action. On a Spark DataFrame, a call such as df.count(), df.collect() or df.write.parquet() that makes Spark run the plan built so far. Unlike pandas, where each step runs as soon as you call it.


Spark: shuffles and slow stages
Narrow transformation. A step each task does on its own partition, so no rows move between partitions: filter, select, withColumn.
Wide transformation. A step that needs rows from other partitions, such as groupBy, orderBy, a window or most joins. Spark adds a shuffle before it.
Shuffle (Exchange). Moving rows between partitions for the next stage: each task writes its rows to its node’s disk, and the next stage’s tasks read them, often from other nodes.
Window query. A step that computes a value over a group of rows and puts it on each row, such as each trip’s payment-type average next to the trip. Every row goes into an Exchange.
Hot key. One join, window or sort value with far more rows than the others. All its rows go to one task, which runs long after the rest of its stage; more nodes do not help.
Spill. Writing to the node’s disk when the rows a task sorts, groups or shuffles do not fit in its share of executor memory. The result is correct but slower.


EMR cluster
Amazon EMR. AWS’s managed service that launches a cluster of EC2 instances with Spark installed. You pay for the nodes from launch until you terminate the cluster.
Primary node. The one EMR instance that runs the cluster manager and the HDFS name service. It runs no executors.
Core node. An EMR instance that runs executors and stores HDFS data. A role an instance plays in the cluster, not a Spark slot.
Task node. An optional EMR instance that runs executors and stores no HDFS data, so it can be removed or bought as spot capacity without losing HDFS data.
HDFS. A file system that splits files into blocks across a cluster’s core nodes’ disks. Its data is lost when the cluster terminates, so our inputs and outputs stay on S3.


Also used on this page
Parquet. A columnar file format. Rows are grouped into blocks that each store every column separately, and metadata at the end of the file says where each part is.
Instance type. The size you pick when you launch an EC2 server: how many vCPUs and how much memory it has, how fast its network is, and whether it has its own local disk.
S3. AWS’s object store. You reach each object over the network by its name inside a bucket, and the data stays with no server running.

title: L4 review: scaling up, scaling out, and where the data lives
text:
Storage side of scaling up

What does each filter condition make Spark read?
A city library keeps its loan records for September to December 2025 in S3 as Parquet, one folder partition per month of loan_date:
s3://city-library/loans/
├── month=2025-09/
│   └── part-0.parquet        about 150 MB
├── month=2025-10/
│   └── part-0.parquet
├── month=2025-11/
│   └── part-0.parquet
└── month=2025-12/
    └── part-0.parquet
Each file holds only its month’s loans, in many row groups (the blocks of rows inside a Parquet file). Inside a file the rows are sorted by branch_id; the other columns, loan_date (a DATE), loan_days and patron_id, are in no particular order. Spark on an EMR cluster runs queries that each have one filter condition. Assume the reader rules out row groups only by their min and max.

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## For each filter condition on the loans folder, what does Spark open and read? Each option may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

- `month = '2025-11'` :: 1 or 2 files opened, every row group read
    > The condition names the folder partition key, so Spark opens the November 2025 folder and rules out the other 3 by their names, without reading their row groups. Every row in the November 2025 file is a November 2025 loan, so every row group is read.
- `month IN ('2025-11', '2025-12')` :: 1 or 2 files opened, every row group read
    > The condition names the folder partition key, so Spark opens the November 2025 and December 2025 folders and rules out the other 2 by their names, without reading their row groups. Every row in those two files is a November 2025 or December 2025 loan, so every row group of both is read.
- `branch_id = 17` :: all 4 files opened, some row groups may be skipped
    > All 4 files are opened, because the condition does not name `month`. Inside each file the rows are sorted by branch, so each row group has a narrow `branch_id` range. Where the writer stored each row group's min and max in the footer, the reader skips the row groups whose range does not include 17, without fetching those row groups.
- `loan_date = DATE '2025-11-14'` :: all 4 files opened, some row groups may be skipped
    > The `month` folders were made from the loan date, but this condition names `loan_date`, so no folder is ruled out by name and Spark opens all 4 files. Each file holds one month's loans, so each row group's `loan_date` min and max fall within that month. In the September 2025, October 2025 and December 2025 files, no row group's range includes 14 November 2025, so where the footer stores each row group's min and max, the reader skips every row group in those files. In the November 2025 file the days are in no order, so every group's range covers the day and every row group is read.
- `loan_days > 21`. Every row group has some loans longer than 21 days :: all 4 files opened, every row group read
    > The condition does not name `month`, so Spark opens all 4 files. Every row group has some loans longer than 21 days, so each row group's maximum `loan_days` is above 21 and the footer rules none out. Without a sort, values usually spread like this, but not always: a row group whose maximum happened to be 21 or less would be skipped.
- `patron_id = 40213` :: all 4 files opened, some row groups may be skipped
    > The condition does not name `month`, so Spark opens all 4 files. The rows are in no order of `patron_id`, so most row groups' min and max will cover 40213 and be read; only a row group whose range happens to miss 40213 is skipped. Sorting by `branch_id` is what lets the `branch_id = 17` row skip most row groups.
- :: footers read, no row group read
    > A footer records where the row groups are and each row group's min and max; the footer holds no rows. Footers alone answer a query only when their min and max rule out every row group. Each condition here leaves at least one row group to read: the `month` conditions name folders that hold loans, the November 2025 file's row groups cover 14 November 2025, and on the unordered columns every row group's min and max cover the value.

Slide: 15, 20, 21, 23, 31


Which folder partition key best supports the analysts’ one-day and one-month queries?
A news site keeps its page views from January 2024 to December 2025 in S3 as one Parquet file, with no folder partitions:
s3://news-site/page-views/
└── page-views.parquet    4 GB, rows sorted by view time, many row groups
The analysts query the file with DuckDB. Their common queries filter on the view time, one day or one month, and count views per article category. The team will rewrite the file into folder partitions on one key, and the analysts will write each time filter so that it also names that key. The rewrite keeps the rows sorted by view time, with many row groups in each file. DuckDB recommends at least 100 MB per folder partition.

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## Which folder partition key best supports the analysts' one-day and one-month queries?

1. [x] `month`: 24 folders of about 170 MB
    > Each query names one month, so it opens one folder. Inside that folder, the footer's minimum and maximum view times let a daily query skip other days' row groups, and each folder partition is over 100 MB. A `day` key would also let a daily query open one folder, but each folder would hold only about 5.5 MB, below DuckDB's 100 MB guidance, and a monthly query would open about 30 of them.
1. [ ] `day`: 731 folders of about 5.5 MB
    > The `day` key matches the daily filter, but each 5.5 MB folder partition is below the 100 MB guidance. A monthly query opens about 30 small folder partitions, one per day of the month, while sorting by view time already lets a daily query skip row groups within a monthly folder partition.
1. [ ] `category`: 12 folders of about 330 MB
    > The queries group by category and filter on dates. Every query needs all 12 categories, so it opens all 12 folders and the key rules nothing out.

Slide: 22–23


Which changes spread the scan over all four threads?
A hotel chain exports its 2025 bookings as one Parquet file:
bookings-2025.parquet     1.2 GB, 30 million rows, one row group
About 2.5 million of the rows are July 2025 bookings. DuckDB with four threads on an m6a.xlarge (4 vCPU, 16 GiB) computes the average nightly price per hotel for July 2025 in 3 s. During the query one vCPU is busy and three stay idle. Every rewrite below writes row groups of about 100,000 rows unless the option says otherwise.

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## Which of these changes let the July query finish sooner by spreading its scan over all four threads? Select every change that does.

- [x] Rewrite the file with row groups of about 100,000 rows
    > At about 100,000 rows each, the 30 million rows make about 300 row groups. DuckDB gives each thread whole row groups to read, so the four threads share the scan.
- [x] Rewrite the bookings file as folder partitions by month, one file per month
    > At about 100,000 rows per row group, the 2.5 million July 2025 rows make about 25 row groups in the July 2025 file. DuckDB gives each thread whole row groups to read, so the four threads share the scan. The query opens only the July 2025 file when its filter names the `month` key; with a filter on the booking date alone, DuckDB opens all twelve files, and their footers rule out the other months' row groups.
- [ ] Rewrite the bookings file as one Parquet file sorted by hotel, still one row group
    > The file has one row group, so one thread reads it and the other three have nothing to read. Sorting changes which rows sit next to each other inside the row group; the file still has one row group for DuckDB to give its threads.
- [ ] Set DuckDB to 32 threads
    > The file has one row group, so one thread reads it and the extra threads have nothing to read. The instance has only 4 vCPUs to run the threads.
- [ ] Move to an m6a.2xlarge (8 vCPU, 32 GiB)
    > The file has one row group, so one thread reads it and the extra vCPUs have nothing to read. More memory does not increase the number of row groups.

Slide: 16–19

section: Scaling out: more nodes, and a network between them
text:
Scaling out: more nodes, and a network between them

Which first change cuts the daily query’s time most?
A parcel company keeps three years of parcel scans as CSV in S3:
s3://parcel-co/scans/
├── part-0.csv
│   …
└── part-N.csv            450 GB in all, 25 columns, 2023 to 2025
A query that runs every day counts late parcels per depot for one month and reads 3 of the 25 columns. On one m6a.xlarge it takes 50 minutes. The instance reads from S3 above its baseline network rate only for the first minutes; for most of the 50 minutes it reads at the m6a.xlarge’s baseline of 1.56 Gbps, about 195 MB/s, and reading all 450 GB at that rate takes about 38 minutes.

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## Which first change is likely to cut the daily query's time most?

1. [x] Convert the CSV once to Parquet
    > The query then fetches only 3 of the 25 columns, compressed and stored as typed values, so most of the 450 GB is not sent over the network. With its data converted to Parquet, L1's taxi query went from 14 min to 5.5 s on one instance. Three nodes cut the time to about a third at best, while reading 3 of 25 columns already cuts the data fetched to about an eighth, before compression, so the Parquet change cuts more.
1. [ ] Run the query on EMR with three m6a.xlarge core nodes
    > Three m6a.xlarge nodes have about three times the network capacity of one, so the query takes at best about a third of the time, and the three nodes still read every byte of the CSV.
1. [ ] Split the CSV into many smaller files
    > Smaller files hold the same 450 GB in total, and every byte is still read over the same network.

Slide: 3, 24, 30, L2 18


Which node type should the team add for this job? *
An EMR cluster with one primary node and two core nodes runs a long Spark job that reads its input from S3 and writes its results back to S3. To finish the job sooner, the team wants to add nodes for it and remove them soon afterwards, without losing any data the cluster stores.

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## Which node type should the team add for this job?

1. [x] Task nodes
    > Task nodes run executors and store no HDFS blocks, so they can be removed as soon as the job ends; the input and the results stay in S3.
1. [ ] Core nodes
    > Core nodes run executors and store HDFS blocks, which exist only on the cluster, so removing a core node risks losing those blocks. The team should not add core nodes for one job and remove them afterwards.
1. [ ] Larger primary node
    > The primary node manages the cluster and coordinates its services. The job's parallel work runs in executors on the core and task nodes, so enlarging the primary adds no capacity for that work.

Slide: 29, L5 18


After how many queries has the rewrite paid back? *
Vancouver publishes its Van311 non-emergency service requests as open data. A team keeps five years of them in S3 as one CSV file per year, and a weekly query reads them all:
s3://van-311/requests/
├── 2021.csv
│   …
└── 2025.csv
Rewriting the CSV files once as sorted Parquet in folder partitions uses 1,200 CPU-seconds. The weekly query uses 50 CPU-seconds on the CSV and 10 CPU-seconds on the rewritten files.

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## After how many weekly queries has the rewrite paid back its CPU-seconds?

1. [x] 30 queries
    > Each query saves 50 − 10 = 40 CPU-seconds, and 1,200 / 40 = 30 weekly runs.
1. [ ] 24 queries
    > 1,200 / 50 divides by what the old query cost. The rewrite is paid back by what each query saves, 40 CPU-seconds.
1. [ ] 120 queries
    > 1,200 / 10 divides by what the new query costs. The rewrite is paid back by what each query saves, 40 CPU-seconds.
1. [ ] 20 queries
    > 1,200 / (50 + 10) adds the two costs together. The rewrite is paid back by what each query saves, 50 − 10 = 40 CPU-seconds.

Slide: 32

section: Case (A2): Best model search for the taxi data
text:
Case (A2): Best model search for the taxi data

Scale up, scale out, or neither? *
Each workload below runs today on one EC2 instance, an m6a.large (2 vCPU, 8 GiB of RAM), unless the row says otherwise. The lecture named these moves for a workload on one instance:
scale up    replace the instance with a larger one
            (more vCPUs, RAM and network on one instance)
scale out   run the work on a cluster of several nodes
neither     keep the one instance as it is

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## Which scaling move does each workload need? Each option may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

- A team of 3 shares a Jupyter environment on the m6a.large and now needs 64 GiB of RAM for a 24 GB dataset :: Scale up
    > One larger instance gives the team the 64 GiB of RAM, so the 24 GB dataset fits on one instance and no cluster is needed.
- Training 100 random forest models with different hyperparameters on a 6 GB dataset takes 12 hours on the largest instance you can get, and the results are needed in 3 hours :: Scale out
    > The models are independent, so they can run on several nodes at once, and no larger instance is available. Four equivalent nodes with ideal scaling give about 3 hours of run time (12 hours / 4). The 3 hours also include the cluster's launch time, so the team needs more than four nodes.
- A dashboard queries a 500 MB SQLite database on the m6a.large :: Neither
    > The 500 MB database fits in the m6a.large's memory and nothing else in the workload needs more, so a larger instance or a cluster would not help the dashboard.
- A weekly report on an m6a.xlarge (16 GiB of RAM) reads 2 of 40 columns from a 7 GB Parquet file and finishes in 20 seconds :: Neither
    > The reader fetches only the 2 columns it needs, and the report already finishes in seconds, so a larger instance or a cluster would not help the report.
- Processing 2 PB of genomic sequencing data from 200 research institutions, which the m6a.large would read through one network link :: Scale out
    > At the m6a.large's baseline of about 0.78 Gbps, about 97 MB/s, one read of 2 PB takes more than 200 days. A larger instance has a faster network link, but one instance stops at the largest size AWS sells. Each node of a cluster adds its own network link and vCPUs and reads and processes part of the data at the same time.
- The m6a.large's 8 GiB of RAM cannot hold a 15 GB Parquet file that a training step needs in memory all at once :: Scale up
    > The training step needs all of the data in one program's memory at once, and a cluster splits the data across the separate memory of each node, so one larger instance is the move that fits. Parquet files are usually compressed and encoded, so the loaded data takes more than 15 GB: pick an instance with well over 15 GB of RAM.
- :: Larger EBS volume
    > None of these workloads is short of disk space. A volume stores files; it adds no RAM, vCPUs or network.

Which time shape of demand does the registration site get?

## A university's course-registration site gets almost no traffic for weeks. When registration opens at 8:00 one morning, about 20,000 students load its pages within ten minutes, and the traffic is back to almost nothing by noon. Which time shape of demand does the site get?

1. [x] Burst

1. [ ] Daily rhythm

title: L4 review: scaling up, scaling out, and where the data lives
text:
Terms used on this page
From the course flashcards, grouped by topic. Practise the terms in quiz mode, or try the match game.

Parquet
Parquet. A columnar file format. Rows are grouped into blocks that each store every column separately, and metadata at the end of the file says where each part is.
Row group. A horizontal block inside one Parquet file, holding one column chunk per column. Its size is set when the file is written, and a file can hold one or many.
Column chunk. The values of one field within one row group of a Parquet file. The writer can store their min and max, which lets a reader skip the whole row group.
Footer. The metadata at the end of a Parquet file: the schema, where each column chunk starts and, if the writer stored them, each chunk’s min and max. A reader fetches it before any data.
Projection pushdown. Handing the reader the list of columns a query uses, so it reads only those columns from a Parquet file.
Predicate pushdown. Handing the reader the query’s filter, so it can skip row groups whose stored min and max show that no row can match.


Layout and files on S3
Folder partition. A dataset layout with one named location per value of a column, such as day=2012-06-14/ (on S3, a prefix). A filter on that column skips the other locations without opening them.
Compaction. Rewriting many small files into fewer, larger ones, so a query opens fewer files. Too few files, or too few row groups, can leave cores idle.
Prefix. The leading part of an object’s name, such as day=2012-06-14/. S3 lists objects by it, and the console’s folders are built from it; the general-purpose buckets we use have no real folders.
S3. AWS’s object store. You reach each object over the network by its name inside a bucket, and the data stays with no server running.
Byte-range read. Asking S3 for one stated part of an object instead of the whole object. Parquet libraries fetch the footer this way, then only the column chunks a query needs.


Memory and resources
Eager load. Reading the whole dataset into memory before the work starts. If data and working space exceed memory, the operating system swaps to disk or stops the program.
Storage, memory, compute and network. The four things every data task uses, each with a capacity and a rate. Looking at a job from each in turn helps find its bottleneck, and cloud architecture often trades one for another.
EBS volume. A disk an EC2 instance reaches over the network, as its main disk or an extra one. Its data survives a stop, and it bills per GB-month while it exists, even when the instance is stopped.


Also used on this page
Instance type. The size you pick when you launch an EC2 server: how many vCPUs and how much memory it has, how fast its network is, and whether it has its own local disk.
Time shape of demand. When a workload asks for its resources across a day or a week: a steady rate, a daily rhythm, a burst, or a scheduled job. With the peak rate, it decides whether provisioned or usage-based billing is cheaper.
Amazon EMR. AWS’s managed service that launches a cluster of EC2 instances with Spark installed. You pay for the nodes from launch until you terminate the cluster.
Primary node (EMR). The one EMR instance that runs the cluster manager and the HDFS name service. It runs no executors.
Core node (EMR). An EMR instance that runs executors and stores HDFS data. A role an instance plays in the cluster, not a Spark slot.
Task node (EMR). An optional EMR instance that runs executors and stores no HDFS data, so it can be removed or bought as spot capacity without losing HDFS data.

title: L1 review: the four resources, and reading only what you need
text:
Data larger than memory

Which ways of reading the file stay within 32 GB of memory? *
An online bookshop exports its orders for January 2020 to December 2025 as one CSV file of 24 GB, with 30 columns. An analyst wants the number of orders and the average order value per country for March 2024. The analyst’s laptop has 32 GB of memory, 8 cores and an SSD with 500 GB free. The analyst works in pandas 2, the version before 3.0.

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## Which of these keep the work within 32 GB of memory while they run? Select every one that does.

- [ ] pandas reads the whole file with `read_csv`, then groups by country
    > An eager load puts the whole file into memory before any grouping. pandas before 3.0 needs about twice the file size in memory because of how pandas stores strings: about 48 GB for the 24 GB file, more than the laptop's 32 GB. The operating system stops the process before the load completes.
- [x] pandas reads 1 million rows at a time, adding each to totals
    > Only one chunk and the running counts and sums per country are in memory at any moment, far below 32 GB. pandas reads all 24 GB, one chunk at a time, and you write the loop yourself.
- [x] DuckDB runs the March 2024 query as SQL on the CSV file
    > One chunk per core and the running counts and sums per country are in memory at any moment, far below 32 GB. DuckDB reads all 24 GB, one chunk at a time on each core, and organizes the loop for you.
- [ ] pandas reads the whole file with `read_csv` from a faster SSD
    > An eager load puts the whole file into memory before any grouping: about 48 GB for the 24 GB file with pandas before 3.0. A faster SSD reads the file sooner, but the load still needs about 48 GB of memory, so the operating system stops the process before the load completes.
- [ ] pandas reads the whole file on an m6a.2xlarge (8 vCPU, 32 GiB)
    > An eager load puts the whole file into memory before any grouping: about 48 GB for the 24 GB file with pandas before 3.0. The instance has 32 GiB, about what the laptop has, so the operating system stops the process there too.

Slide: 4, 6, 8 (also 3, 22)

section: Parquet on S3: reading only what you need
text:
Parquet on S3: reading only what you need

May 2025 downloads: reading the file over the network
A podcast platform keeps its episode downloads for January 2024 to December 2025 as one Parquet file in S3:
downloads.parquet    4.8 GB, 40 columns, each column about 120 MB of the file
                     rows sorted by download time
                     24 row groups of about equal size, one per month, 200 MB each
A query counts downloads per episode for May 2025 and uses 6 of the 40 columns. The footer at the end of the file holds each row group’s min and max download time.

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## DuckDB on a laptop reads downloads.parquet directly from S3 using `httpfs`, its extension for reading remote files. About how many MB does it fetch for the May 2025 query, not counting the footer?

1. [x] 30 MB
    > The footer's min and max show that only 1 of the 24 row groups holds May 2025, and from it DuckDB fetches only the 6 columns' chunks: 6 × 120 MB / 24 = 30 MB. DuckDB reads the footer first and works out which byte ranges hold those chunks. S3 returns only the byte ranges DuckDB asks for, and S3 itself does not choose columns or rows.
1. [ ] 720 MB
    > 720 MB is the 6 columns from all 24 row groups. The rows are sorted by download time, so the footer's min and max rule out the 23 row groups that hold no May 2025 downloads.
1. [ ] 200 MB
    > 200 MB is every column of the May row group, as if a row group had to be read in full. Each column has its own chunk inside the row group, so DuckDB does not fetch the other 34 columns.
1. [ ] 4,800 MB
    > Fetching 4,800 MB means reading every row group and every column. The rows are sorted by download time, so the footer's min and max rule out the 23 row groups that hold no May 2025 downloads. Each column has its own chunk, so DuckDB does not fetch the other 34 columns.

The platform then rewrites the same downloads into a new file of the same size, with the rows not ordered by time: each of the 24 row groups now holds downloads from all 24 months. The columns, their sizes and the query stay the same.

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## About how many MB does DuckDB fetch from the rewritten file for the May 2025 query, not counting the footer?

1. [x] 720 MB
    > Every row group's min and max now span all 24 months, so none can be ruled out. DuckDB still fetches only the 6 columns' chunks: 6 × 120 MB = 720 MB.
1. [ ] 30 MB
    > Choosing 30 MB assumes that one row group holds all of May 2025, as in the sorted file. In the rewritten file every row group's min and max span all 24 months, so none can be ruled out and DuckDB fetches the 6 columns' chunks from all 24 row groups.
1. [ ] 200 MB
    > Choosing 200 MB assumes that one row group still holds all of May and must be read in full. In the rewritten file every row group's min and max span all 24 months, so none can be ruled out, and DuckDB fetches only the 6 columns' chunks, from all 24 row groups.
1. [ ] 4,800 MB
    > Every row group must now be read, and each column still has its own chunk in every row group, so DuckDB fetches only the 6 columns' chunks and not the whole file.

Slide: 12, 13, 14 (also 9, 10; L4 slide 20 for sorting)

title: L1 review: the four resources, and reading only what you need
text:
Pattern of use

Which resource is the bottleneck of each job? *
Each job below runs on a laptop with this setup:
memory     16 GB
compute    8 cores and a GPU
storage    an SSD with 500 GB free, which reads and writes about 2 GB/s
network    a home connection of 100 Mbps, about 12 MB/s

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## Which resource is the bottleneck of each job? Each option may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

- Gradient boosting with 2,000 trees on a 4 GB table in memory; one core is at 100% for 5 hours :: compute
    > The trees are built one after another, because each tree depends on the last. The work inside each tree can be split across cores; this run uses one core, which stays at 100% the whole time. The 4 GB table fits in memory, and storage and network do not limit the job, so that core is the bottleneck.
- Turning 500 hours of recorded interviews into text with a speech model on the laptop's GPU, which stays at 100% for the whole run :: compute
    > The GPU stays at 100% the whole time. The SSD reads the recordings much faster than the model processes them, so the GPU is the bottleneck.
- A dashboard downloads a whole 6 GB Parquet file from S3 on every refresh, and each refresh takes about 8 minutes :: network
    > At 12 MB/s, transferring 6 GB takes about 8 minutes, so the network connection is the bottleneck. Reading only the needed columns and row groups would reduce the amount of data transferred over the network.
- Copying 350 GB of satellite images from S3 to the SSD; the copy takes about 8 hours :: network
    > At 12 MB/s, transferring 350 GB takes about 8 hours, so the network connection is the bottleneck. The SSD has enough space and can write much faster than the network can deliver data.
- A pandas pivot turns a 5 GB sales table into a wide table of about 22 GB; the SSD stays busy as the operating system moves data from memory to the SSD, and then the operating system stops the process running the pivot :: memory
    > The wide table alone is larger than the 16 GB of memory, so the operating system stops the process before the pivot completes. The SSD is busy only because memory is full and the operating system moves data from memory to the SSD, so the bottleneck is memory.
- Fitting a model that must hold every row of its 24 GB feature table at once :: memory
    > Every row is needed at the same time, so there is nothing to skip: 24 GB does not fit in 16 GB of memory.
- :: storage
    > The SSD has space for every file here and reads about 2 GB/s, faster than any of these jobs needs. In the pivot, the SSD is busy only because memory is full and the operating system moves data from memory to the SSD; memory is the bottleneck.

Who is responsible for what

On a managed database service, who is responsible for what?
Your research team stores its survey responses in a managed database service on AWS, a platform as a service (PaaS): you create tables, load the data and write SQL queries, and pay for the service by the hour.

## On the managed database service, who is responsible for each of these? Each option may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

- The disks the tables are stored on, and replacing them when they fail :: AWS
    > On a managed database service, AWS is responsible for everything from the hardware up to the database engine. The disks are part of the hardware, so replacing a failed disk is not your responsibility.
- The operating system under the database engine, and its patches :: AWS
    > On a managed database service, AWS is responsible for everything from the hardware up to the database engine. Patching the operating system is not your responsibility.
- Keeping the database engine running, and restarting it after a failure :: AWS
    > On a managed database service, AWS is responsible for everything from the hardware up to the database engine. Restarting the engine after a failure is not your responsibility.
- The design of the tables and the SQL queries run against them :: you
    > The table design and the SQL queries are your responsibility. AWS is responsible for keeping the database engine running; how you organize and query the data is your responsibility.
- Which survey responses are loaded, and keeping them correct :: you
    > Choosing which survey responses to load, and keeping them complete and correct, is your responsibility. AWS is responsible for storing the responses and running your queries over them; checking that the responses are correct is your responsibility.

text:
Terms used on this page
From the course flashcards, grouped by topic. Practise them in quiz mode, or try the match game.

Memory and resources
Storage, memory, compute and network. The four things every data task uses, each with a capacity and a rate. Looking at a job from each in turn helps find its bottleneck, and cloud architecture often trades one for another.
Eager load. Reading the whole dataset into memory before the work starts. If data and working space exceed memory, the operating system swaps to disk or stops the program.


Parquet
Parquet. A columnar file format. Rows are grouped into blocks that each store every column separately, and metadata at the end of the file says where each part is.
Row group. A horizontal block inside one Parquet file, holding one column chunk per column. Its size is set when the file is written, and a file can hold one or many.
Column chunk. The values of one field within one row group of a Parquet file. The writer can store their min and max, which lets a reader skip the whole row group.
Footer. The metadata at the end of a Parquet file: the schema, where each column chunk starts and, if the writer stored them, each chunk’s min and max. A reader fetches it before any data.
Projection pushdown. Handing the reader the list of columns a query uses, so it reads only those columns from a Parquet file.
Predicate pushdown. Handing the reader the query’s filter, so it can skip row groups whose stored min and max show that no row can match.


Files on S3
S3. AWS’s object store. You reach each object over the network by its name inside a bucket, and the data stays with no server running.
Byte-range read. Asking S3 for one stated part of an object instead of the whole object. Parquet libraries fetch the footer this way, then only the column chunks a query needs.


Also used on this page
Instance (EC2). A virtual machine you rent from AWS, billed per second for the time it runs. Stopping it ends the compute charge, but its EBS disk still bills.
Instance type. The size you pick when you launch an EC2 server: how many vCPUs and how much memory it has, how fast its network is, and whether it has its own local disk.
Cost granularity. The unit a provider bills in, such as one second of instance time or one request. With per-second billing, a faster, pricier instance can come out cheaper per task.

title: L3 review: cost models, capacity and what starts a function
text:
What starts a function

Requests, events and schedules
A regional food bank keeps its pantry records in an S3 bucket and runs each job below on AWS. Pantries upload each day’s check-ins as a CSV file to checkins/incoming/. S3 sends its object-created events to EventBridge, Amazon’s service whose rules use an event pattern or a schedule to start a target such as a function.

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## What starts each job? Each option may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

- recomputes a pantry's month each time the pantry uploads a corrected file to `checkins/corrections/` :: event, matched by an EventBridge rule's event pattern
    > A new corrected file is an event; the rule's pattern matches new objects under `checkins/corrections/`, and nobody waits for the result.
- every 30 minutes, fetches a public food-price list from a provincial web service and appends it to a CSV in S3 :: schedule, from an EventBridge rule's schedule expression
    > The schedule starts the function every 30 minutes, and no new file or caller is involved; the function then makes the web request. The rule's schedule expression, such as `rate(30 minutes)`, says when.
- answers a volunteer's phone form, which sends a household's postal code to the web address the HTTP API gives the function and waits for the nearest open pantry :: request, through API Gateway's HTTP API
    > A volunteer's phone form sends a request and waits for the answer. API Gateway gives the function a web address, and each request to that address becomes one call of the function.
- answers a coordinator's Python script, which calls the web address the HTTP API gives the function with a start and an end date and waits :: request, through API Gateway's HTTP API
    > The request comes from a coordinator's Python script rather than a browser, and the script waits for the answer. API Gateway gives the function a web address, and each request to that address becomes one call of the function.
- :: a direct call from a volunteer's laptop
    > A call from a person's laptop is still a request, but no job in this scenario calls the function directly. The form and the script reach the function through the HTTP API's web address, while the other jobs start from EventBridge event or schedule rules.

A parks department keeps its inventory of 150,000 street trees as Parquet in S3. Staff open a web page that asks a Lambda function, through API Gateway’s HTTP API, for a yearly report on one neighbourhood’s trees, and the page waits for the answer. The function’s timeout is set to 5 minutes. Each report takes the function about 50 seconds to build. The function’s logs show every report finished, yet the page shows an error every time.

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## Which change gets the staff their reports?

1. [x] Start the build from an S3 event; the page fetches the result
    > API Gateway's HTTP API must answer a request within 30 seconds, and that limit cannot be raised. The page can instead upload a small request file under `requests/`; its object-created event starts the function, which writes the report under `results/` for the page to fetch after the 50-second build.
1. [ ] Raise the function's timeout from 5 minutes to 15 minutes
    > The function already finishes in 50 seconds, before its 5-minute timeout, so raising that timeout does not help. API Gateway's HTTP API has stopped waiting at 30 seconds.
1. [ ] Buy provisioned concurrency so that no call has to wait for a cold start
    > A cold start is the setup delay when AWS creates a new execution environment, but avoiding it does not remove the 50 seconds needed to build the report. Provisioned concurrency keeps execution environments initialised before calls and can save one to a few seconds of setup time.

Slide: 5, 9, 13 (also 8, 10, 41)


Pulling a partner’s nightly file
A community science group collects bird counts from a partner society. The partner publishes a new CSV of the previous day’s counts on its own website by 06:30 each morning, and sends no notice when it does. Each pull finishes within five minutes. The group wants each file in its S3 bucket by 08:00 and does not want responsibility for an instance.

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## Which way of starting the pull function meets the group's needs?

1. [x] Schedule: an EventBridge rule starts it once an hour
    > The partner's website sends no event, so the group needs a clock-based trigger. With the file available by 06:30, an hourly schedule starts the pull function again by about 07:30, and the five-minute pull leaves time before 08:00. An EventBridge schedule expression such as `rate(1 hour)` supplies that trigger.
1. [ ] Event: an EventBridge rule starts it when the partner's file appears
    > This option treats the partner's website as if it were the group's bucket. An event needs something that reports the change; S3 reports new objects in the group's own bucket, and the partner's site reports nothing.
1. [ ] Request: the partner's website calls the function's web address
    > This option needs the partner to change its website to call the group's function. Nothing in the setup says the partner will make that change, and the group does not control the partner's site.

section: Inside a function: the handler and its environment
text:
Inside a function: the handler and its environment

How many times does each line run?
A bakery chain answers “how much did this store sell yesterday?” with a Lambda function behind API Gateway’s HTTP API. The function’s file is:
import json, duckdb
con = duckdb.connect()
con.execute("LOAD httpfs;")                 # from the function's layer

def lambda_handler(event, context):
    store = event["queryStringParameters"]["store"]
    total = con.execute(
        "SELECT sum(amount) FROM read_parquet('s3://bakery-sales/yesterday.parquet') WHERE store = ?",
        [store]).fetchone()[0]
    return {"statusCode": 200, "body": json.dumps({"store": store, "total": total})}
The file leaves out the line that gives DuckDB the function’s credentials for S3.
On Friday 16 October 2026 the function answers 1,200 calls, and its logs show that AWS set up 3 execution environments for them that day.

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## On that Friday, how many times does each line run? Each option may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

- `con = duckdb.connect()` :: 3 times
    > The line runs once in each of the 3 execution environments because it is module-level code outside `lambda_handler`, and module-level code runs once when an environment is set up. Later calls in that environment can reuse the connection until AWS removes the environment.
- `con.execute("LOAD httpfs;")` :: 3 times
    > The line runs once in each of the 3 execution environments because it is module-level code outside `lambda_handler`, and module-level code runs once when an environment is set up. Later calls in that environment can use the loaded extension until AWS removes the environment.
- `store = event["queryStringParameters"]["store"]` :: 1,200 times
    > The line runs once for each of the 1,200 calls because it is inside `lambda_handler`, and each call starts `lambda_handler` once; each call's `event` carries its own store.
- the `SELECT sum(amount)` query :: 1,200 times
    > The query runs once for each of the 1,200 calls because it is inside `lambda_handler`, and each call starts `lambda_handler` once; the query uses that call's store.
- `return {...}` :: 1,200 times
    > The return line runs once for each of the 1,200 calls because it is inside `lambda_handler`, and each call starts `lambda_handler` once; each call returns an answer for API Gateway to send to the caller.
- :: 1,197 times
    > This option counts only the warm calls, as if the first call in a new environment did not run the handler. A call with a cold start runs the module-level code and then the handler, so the handler lines run 1,200 times.

text:
Same pipeline on bigger data

Which change keeps the compaction’s memory from growing?
A farmers’ market co-op collects its vendors’ card sales. Every 15 minutes the payment provider uploads a CSV of the new sales, about 2,000 rows, to S3, and the upload’s event starts a Lambda function with a 1,024 MB memory setting. The function reads the co-op’s single Parquet file of all sales since June 2026 into pandas, adds the new rows, and writes the whole file back. In August 2026 the function starts to fail: it runs out of memory.

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## Which change keeps the compaction's memory from growing as the months go by?

1. [x] Write each day's rows to one file per `day=` folder
    > With one file per day, such as `sales-daily/day=2026-08-14/part.parquet`, each run reads and rewrites at most one day's rows, so the function uses about the same memory in December 2026 as in June 2026. DuckDB can still read the day folders back as one table (slide 30).
1. [ ] Raise the memory setting to 10,240 MB, the most Lambda allows
    > A larger memory setting delays the failure, but the single file continues to grow until it reaches the new limit. Lambda's price also depends on the memory setting: each second of a call would be charged as ten times as many GB-seconds.
1. [ ] Do the same merge with DuckDB instead of with pandas
    > DuckDB uses less memory than pandas for the same rows and can spill to `/tmp`, but a run that reads and rewrites the whole history still needs more memory each month, because the file grows every month.

Function or an instance for each workload
A city’s data team runs the workloads below. ## For each workload, what should run it? Each option may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

- a summer-camp sign-up page: almost nothing for months, then 30,000 requests in the 3 minutes after sign-up opens on 2 March 2026; an answer may take up to 3 seconds :: Lambda function, one call per request
    > During the idle months, Lambda's request and GB-second charges stop, while AWS can start many execution environments for the burst; the allowed 3-second response time leaves room for cold starts. The busiest hour has 30,000 calls, below the 50,000-an-hour crossover, so Lambda costs less than an instance, which AWS would also charge for during the idle months. An instance created only for sign-up day would leave the few requests of the other months with nothing to answer them, and one instance would queue the 30,000 requests that arrive in 3 minutes.
- a staff lookup page: about 3,000 calls an hour at midday, near zero overnight :: Lambda function, one call per request
    > The page's busiest hour has 3,000 calls, below the 50,000-an-hour crossover, so the function costs less than the instance at the peak, and the function's cost drops close to zero overnight as the call rate falls.
- a monthly 20-minute job that needs 40 GB of memory at once and cannot be split :: instance for the run only
    > 40 GB is past a function's 10,240 MB limit, and 20 minutes is past a call's 15-minute limit. Ephemeral infrastructure means creating the instance for the job and deleting it afterward, so AWS charges only for the monthly run.
- a weekly 10-minute join that needs 24 GB of memory at once and cannot be split into smaller calls :: instance for the run only

- :: always-on instance

The request workloads here stay below the 50,000-an-hour crossover, and the scheduled jobs run for minutes a week or a month, so AWS would charge for an always-on instance during mostly idle hours. An always-on instance suits a service that must stay up and keep data in memory between requests, such as the JupyterHub instance on slide 39. No workload here needs either.

title: L3 review: cost models, capacity and what starts a function
text:
Terms used on this page
From the course flashcards, grouped by topic. Practise them in quiz mode, or try the match game.

Triggers: what starts a function
Request (trigger). A call that asks a Lambda function for an answer while the caller waits for it, such as a browser going through API Gateway.
Event (trigger). A report that something happened, such as a new object landing in a bucket. A Lambda function processes it with no caller waiting for an answer.
EventBridge. The AWS service whose rules match things that happen, such as a new object in a bucket, or fire on a clock, and send each match to a target such as a Lambda function.
API Gateway. The AWS service that gives a function a web address, so a browser or a program can call it over HTTP. Its simplest kind waits at most 30 seconds for an answer.


Inside a Lambda function
Lambda function. The unit you deploy to AWS Lambda: your code and its settings, run each time a trigger fires. One setting, memory, also sets its CPU and its price per millisecond.
Handler. The function in your code that Lambda calls on each invocation, taking event and context. Code outside it runs once per environment, so a client built there is reused.
Execution environment. The isolated space AWS sets up to run a Lambda function, with its memory and a temporary disk. AWS may reuse it for later calls and pauses it between them.
Cold start. The set-up before the first call in a new Lambda environment: AWS loads the code, then your code’s initialisation runs, such as opening connections and importing libraries.
Execution role. The identity AWS takes on when it runs a Lambda function. It decides which resources the code may read or change.


Cost models
Provisioned capacity. Compute you pay for while it is allocated to you, used or not. Unlike pay-per-use compute, its charge continues when nothing runs.
Usage-based billing. Charges for measured work, such as each request or each millisecond a function runs. They stop when nothing runs; stored data and logs still cost money.
Idle test. The question to ask of each compute charge: does it bill while nothing runs? If yes, it is provisioned capacity. Storage and logs are counted separately.
Time shape of demand. When a workload asks for its resources across a day or a week: a steady rate, a daily rhythm, a burst, or a scheduled job. With the peak rate, it decides whether provisioned or usage-based billing is cheaper.
Ephemeral infrastructure. A server or cluster created for one piece of work and deleted after it, so it bills only around that work. Our EMR clusters were launched for a run and terminated after.
Instance (EC2). A virtual machine you rent from AWS, billed per second for the time it runs. Stopping it ends the compute charge, but its EBS disk still bills.


Also used on this page
Serverless. A service model where the platform runs and scales your code and you never pick or patch the computers under it. It usually bills per request and running time; stored data still costs money.
Compaction. Rewriting many small files into fewer, larger ones, so a query opens fewer files. Too few files, or too few row groups, can leave cores idle.
Folder partition. A dataset layout with one named location per value of a column, such as day=2012-06-14/ (on S3, a prefix). A filter on that column skips the other locations without opening them.
Prefix (S3). The leading part of an object’s name, such as day=2012-06-14/. S3 lists objects by it, and the console’s folders are built from it; the general-purpose buckets we use have no real folders.
Parquet. A columnar file format. Rows are grouped into blocks that each store every column separately, and metadata at the end of the file says where each part is.
